exact_edits.old: [F1] A smooth complete curve is determined by its function field, and a curve with a $k$-point whose base change to $k^{\mathrm a}$ is $\mathbf P^1$ has function field $k(t)$, hence is $\mathbf P^1$ (Milne, Ch. 20); the automorphism group of $\mathbf P^1$ is $\operatorname{PGL}_2$, with the natural action on lines of the standard representation and $\operatorname{PGL}_2\to\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf P^1)$ an isomorphism (Milne, Ch. 20). The projective linear group is $\mathrm{GL}_2/\mathbf G_m$ ([[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]]).
exact_edits.new: [F1] A regular complete connected curve is determined by its function field; a curve with a $k$-point whose base change to $k^{\mathrm a}$ is $\mathbf P^1$ is $\mathbf P^1$ over $k$ (Milne, §§20.2-20.4). The latter is the genus-zero splitting assertion used in (a).

[F4] The matrix supplier [[lem-general-linear-group-scheme-and-its-coordinate-ring]] identifies $\mathrm{GL}_2(R)$ with invertible matrices and $\mathbf G_m(R)$ with $R^\times$. Projective space of lines is $\mathbf P_{\mathrm{lines}}(W)=\mathbb P(W^\vee)$; its test-scheme points are rank-one locally direct summand subbundles of $W$, and a linear representation acts by transporting those subbundles ([[lem-projective-space-action-from-linear-representation]], [[thm-projective-bundle-represents-line-quotients]]). Use the usual relative projective charts ([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]]). Here $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ means the represented fppf quotient of $\mathrm{GL}_2$ by its central scalar $\mathbf G_m$, in the sense of [[def-quotient-sheaf-and-representable-quotient]], not the naive quotient of points over arbitrary rings; Milne, Example 5.49, gives this definition, and Proposition 20.7 with Lemmas 20.8-20.9 gives the automorphism identification. Steps 2.2-2.5 construct the quotient and prove that identification over every $k$-algebra.

exact_edits.old: 2.1 For (b), base change to an algebraic closure. The action remains transitive on the positive-dimensional curve and is therefore nontrivial; [F2] gives $C_{k^{\mathrm a}}\cong\mathbf P^1$. The assumed $k$-point and step 1.1 then give $C\cong\mathbf P^1$ over $k$. The action of $\mathrm{GL}_2$ on lines has scalar kernel and induces the group-scheme isomorphism $\mathrm{PGL}_2\cong\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf P^1)$: over every $k$-algebra $R$, an automorphism preserves $\mathcal O(1)$ up to a line bundle pulled back from $\operatorname{Spec}R$. Trivializing that line bundle locally gives an invertible transformation of the rank-two space of sections, up to scalar. These local transformations glue in $\mathrm{PGL}_2$, and scalar matrices give exactly the kernel. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]
exact_edits.new:
2.1 For (b), base change to an algebraic closure. The action remains transitive on the positive-dimensional curve and is therefore nontrivial; [F2] gives $C_{k^{\mathrm a}}\cong\mathbf P^1$. The assumed $k$-point and step 1.1 then give $C\cong\mathbf P^1$ over $k$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Put $Q=D_+(ad-bc)\subset\mathbf P_{\mathrm{lines}}(M_2(k))\cong\mathbf P^3_k$, where $a,b,c,d$ are the matrix entries. A test-scheme point of $Q$ is a line subbundle of matrices whose local generators have invertible determinant. Thus it is Zariski locally represented by an invertible matrix $A$, and any two generators of the same line differ by a unit scalar. Conversely an invertible matrix has unimodular entries, since its determinant is a unit, and spans such a line. Matrix multiplication and the adjugate give compatible morphisms on these local representatives, independent of scalar rescaling; they define multiplication and inverse on $Q$, with identity the line of $I_2$. The map $\mathrm{GL}_2\to Q$ is locally a trivial $\mathbf G_m$-torsor: on a projective chart normalize the corresponding matrix entry to $1$, and every lift is its unit scalar multiple. Consequently $Q$ represents the fppf quotient $\mathrm{GL}_2/\mathbf G_m$, hence is $\operatorname{PGL}_2$. Its action on $\mathbf P^1$ is locally $[x:y]\mapsto[ax+by:cx+dy]$. [F4, construct, algebra]

2.3 Let $R$ be any $k$-algebra and $\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}_R(\mathbf P^1_R)$. The three sections $P_0=\alpha(0)$, $P_1=\alpha(1)$ and $P_\infty=\alpha(\infty)$ remain pairwise distinct in every residue field. Zariski locally on $\operatorname{Spec}R$, choose generators $p_0,p_1,p_\infty\in R^2$ of their line subbundles. The matrix $A=(p_\infty,p_0)$ is invertible, because its determinant is nonzero modulo every maximal ideal. Write $A^{-1}p_1=(u,v)^t$. Distinctness from $P_0$ and $P_\infty$ implies that $u$ and $v$ are units. Hence $M=A\operatorname{diag}(u,v)$ sends $0,1,\infty$ to $P_0,P_1,P_\infty$, respectively. Set $\beta=M^{-1}\alpha$; it fixes the three standard sections. [F4, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

2.4 A three-section-fixing automorphism $\beta$ is the identity even when $R$ has nilpotents. Fixing $0$ and $\infty$ preserves the two affine charts and their section ideals, so its coordinate homomorphisms have the forms $T\mapsto a_1T+T^2P_2(T)$ and $T^{-1}\mapsto b_1T^{-1}+T^{-2}Q_2(T^{-1})$. The induced automorphisms of the section ideals modulo their squares make $a_1,b_1$ units. On the overlap the two images multiply to $1$, so $a_1b_1+b_1TP_2+a_1T^{-1}Q_2+P_2Q_2=1$. If $P_2\ne0$, the highest exponent of $b_1TP_2$ exceeds all exponents in the other nonconstant terms and has a nonzero coefficient because $b_1$ is a unit, a contradiction. Thus $P_2=0$; the lowest-exponent argument gives $Q_2=0$. Fixing $1$ then gives $a_1=b_1=1$, so $\beta$ is the identity on both charts. [F4, algebra]

2.5 It follows from steps 2.3-2.4 that every $\alpha$ is locally induced by an invertible matrix. A matrix inducing the identity must fix $0$ and $\infty$, hence be diagonal with unit entries, and fixing $1$ makes these entries equal. Thus the kernel is exactly the scalar $\mathbf G_m$, over every base ring. Local matrices inducing $\alpha$ differ by unit scalars on overlaps, so their classes glue in the quotient $Q$ of step 2.2. This gives a natural bijection $Q(R)\cong\operatorname{Aut}_R(\mathbf P^1_R)$ for every $R$, compatible with composition, and hence the claimed isomorphism of $k$-group schemes and faithful action. Over the field $k$, each matrix line has a global generator, giving $\operatorname{Aut}_k(\mathbf P^1_k)=\mathrm{GL}_2(k)/k^\times$; over general $R$, the quotient is understood as the sheaf quotient. [F4, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, algebra]

independent_reasoning: The triple-matching matrix uses generators only locally. An arbitrary R-point of PGL2 can involve a nontrivial line bundle, so global matrix representatives are not asserted.

The rigidity proof explicitly proves a1,b1 are units using the section ideals modulo their squares. This makes the highest/lowest Laurent-coefficient argument valid over rings with zero divisors and nilpotents; a degree argument without unit leading coefficients would be invalid.
Q points are projective lines of matrices, not merely global matrices modulo R^times. The local scalar-torsor description supplies sheafification and group-scheme representability.

The action kernel is scalar as a scheme: fixing the standard sections over every R forces a scalar matrix. Surjectivity is shown for all R via local lifts and gluing, not inferred from algebraically closed field points.
